extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent practitioners and solicitors advising on obtaining letters patent (United Kingdom, early 19th-century practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance on the procedure, drafting, and judicial construction of letters patent in the United Kingdom, including specification requirements, fees, oppositions, and post-grant property issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and fair disclosure in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: To support a patent, it is necessary that the specification should make a full and fair disclosure to the public of all that is known to the patentee respecting his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not disclose what the patentee knows about the invention, the consideration on which the patent is obtained fails. Courts have held non-disclosure of known useful matter to be 'bad.'

rubrics_metrics.name: No misrepresentation of multiple competent means
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee 'represents several things as competent to produce a specific effect, when only one will answer, that is bad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must not claim multiple alternatives as effective when only one actually works; presenting useless alternatives can invalidate the patent or be viewed unfavourably by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No suppression of known effective means
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee 'suppresses any thing which he knows will answer, that also is bad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealing a known way that will accomplish the invention is a defect in the specification and undermines the patent's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (statutory) is the primary condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Under statute (21 Jac. 1, c. 3, s.6) the condition required is that the thing shall be new, not that it shall be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While utility has sometimes been left to a jury, satisfying the statutory novelty requirement is the primary statutory condition for the grant of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent may fail if part of claim is not new
rubrics_metrics.description: There are authorities that where a patent is granted for several things, and one of them is not new, the patent 'fails in toto.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have sometimes held that inclusion of non‑novel elements among claimed items can invalidate the whole grant, though holdings vary by case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose improvements made before enrolment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of a person taking out a patent to communicate to the public any improvement that he may make upon his invention before the specification has been enrolled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee improves the invention between taking out the patent and enrolling the specification, those improvements (if made by him) must be communicated in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for making and enrolling the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The time allowed for making and enrolling the specification (commonly six months) is too long and enables fraud; proposed reduction to one month for each kingdom and two months for the United Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter statutory time limits reduce opportunities for fraud and for intervening third-party improvements to arise before disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of specification may be by proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement of the specification is required to be made in person, but allowing it by power of attorney would cause no injury; representatives should be allowed when inventor is ill or dies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural flexibility is desirable: allow power of attorney or representatives to file when inventors are abroad, ill, or deceased, with safeguards (imperfect specs could be open to repeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted deposit of models and judicial correction of immaterial parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit a model to be deposited in some public building, and enact that all immaterial parts in the description might be altered by the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposited models assist public understanding; judges should be empowered to correct immaterial descriptive errors without depriving patentee of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may amend clerical enrolment errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When a clerical error should creep into the enrolment of the specification, the Court will interfere on motion, and order the enrolment to be amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial remedies exist for formal mistakes in enrolment; such correction preserves the substance of valid patents despite clerical slips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of inventor unnecessary and leads to perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: The affidavit that the petitioner is the inventor is an unnecessary oath; it leads to perjury and is not a safeguard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends replacing affidavits with less onerous notices and allowing assignment so assignees can take patents in their own names, eliminating the need for such affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify petition/notice and centralize fee payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor might present a petition with a notice (not an affidavit) and deposit half the fees at one patent office rather than attend several government offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizing procedures and fee payments would reduce cost and delay; titles should be published in the Gazette to give public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees are excessive and duplicative; should vary by term
rubrics_metrics.description: Present fees are very heavy; the amount should be reduced (majority view ~one half) and the amount might vary according to the length of the privilege granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicative charges across multiple official stages are wasteful; reducing fees and charging pro rata by term would lower cost and reduce professional assistance needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional fees for extension to colonies and extra names criticized (possibly illegal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges of additional fees for additional names, and further fees if the grant is extended to the colonies, appear to be illegal and are heavily criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes examples of small procedural additions (e.g., adding the phrase 'and colonies') being charged large fees—an administrative abuse to be reformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat system causes fraud and should be abolished
rubrics_metrics.description: The caveat, as at present formed, is the grand source of all the frauds which torment real inventors; the system must be abolished altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats generate multiple oppositions and burdensome expense for true inventors; instead, when a title appears in the Gazette, parties should apply to the Attorney General within one month for redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppositions/hearings impose heavy fees and delay
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent is opposed, parties pay substantial fees to clerks and to the Attorney General for hearings; numerous oppositions can cost inventors very large sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice of many oppositions before officials increases cost and uncertainty; the author cites examples where oppositions imposed heavy fees on inventors and enriched office-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative reform: Patent Office under Attorney General and expedited priority resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office for patents should be remodelled; the Attorney General should head it with power to appoint sufficient officers and decide questions of priority of invention; one month should be allowed to lay complaints before the Attorney General and the date of petition should be the date of the letters patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized, expert administration would reduce delay, limit abuses by intermediaries, and provide faster, authoritative resolution of priority disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction favouring the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent are provided to be 'taken, construed, and adjudged in the most favourable and beneficial sense, for the best advantage of the patentee and his assigns' notwithstanding not full and certain description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern judicial tendency (at time of writing) is to make reasonable intendments in favour of patentees; legislators should expressly require courts to adopt the construction most favourable to patentees and permit correction of unintentional formal errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on retrospective effect of later specifications/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A later statute or specification substituted by statute cannot operate retrospectively to enable a patentee to say he possessed earlier matter that he did not possess at the date of the first patent; a later improvement not existing at original date cannot be treated as then known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not allow an act of parliament or later enrolled specification to supply matter that was not in the original possession or discovery at the time of the earlier patent; such retrospective expansion may invalidate the grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in patent: assignment and bankruptcy consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent pass to the assignees of a bankrupt; an act provided that if the privilege became vested in more than five persons then the patent would cease, but courts held that clause applied to voluntary assignment, not assignment by operation of law (bankruptcy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory clauses limiting number of persons entitled to a patent can have complex effects; bankruptcy assignments pass patent rights to assignees notwithstanding some statutory limits framed for voluntary assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing issues require legislative regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many questions respecting the power of granting licences (whether patentees can grant licences to companies of more than five persons, licences for particular districts, and regranting licences) will not be satisfactorily settled until legislative enactments regulate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware of uncertainties in licence scope and enforceability under existing law; legislative clarification is advisable.
